25.0.s.en: (2) The victory over Edom and Amaziah's apostasy

25.0.0.en: Amaziah prepared to fight Edom, and the men of his army succeeded, numbering 300,000 warriors trained for war. This number is small compared with the army of the kingdom of Judah about fifty years earlier, in the days of his grandfather Jehoshaphat, when they numbered about one million two hundred thousand (2 Chr 17:14-18). The smallness of the army may be due to the absence of God's blessing, because most of the kings after Jehoshaphat were wicked. But why did Amaziah prepare to fight Edom? Perhaps Edom threatened war, or gathered armies on the border, so Amaziah was forced to prepare for war, and he found his army small. What would he do? This will appear in the next verse.

25.1.0.en: A talent of silver: The talent had different weights, ranging between 17 and 40 kg.

25.1.1.en: Amaziah sought the help of mercenary soldiers to assist him in the war, and he paid for them a hundred talents of silver. They were from the tribe of Ephraim, from the kingdom of Israel, since this tribe was large and known for its military strength.

25.2.0.en: God's love appeared in His sending a prophet, whose name is not mentioned, who declared to King Amaziah that he should not take help from the army of the kingdom of Israel, because they were wicked, worshipping idols, and God was not with them, and it is not right to take help from the wicked. By this the prophet showed Amaziah the weakness of his faith, because he did not trust in God, who helps the weak, but went to trust in men, and even in the wicked.

25.3.0.en: The prophet asked Amaziah to go alone, and God would support him, however weak he was; but if he trusted in the wicked, he would be defeated and fall, whereas if he trusted in God, he would surely be victorious, because victory is by the power of the Lord.

25.3.1.en: At the beginning of the verse God plainly commands Amaziah to be strong and to go alone to fight; the second part shows him that he will fall if he goes with the army of Israel; then in the third part of the verse it returns to show that God has the power to help, so Amaziah does not need the help of the wicked.

25.4.0.en: Amaziah felt a great loss if he did not take an army from the tribe of Ephraim, because he had already paid the sum of 100 talents of silver. He was ready to obey God, but he was thinking of the large sum that he had paid and had not benefited from. Here the prophet answered him that God is able to compensate him for this sum, but he must carry out God's word and not take help from the wicked.

25.5.0.en: Amaziah's obedience to God appeared in his dismissing the army of Ephraim and accepting the loss of the huge sum he had paid them, which was a hundred talents. On the other hand, the army of Ephraim murmured bitterly against Amaziah, for they considered their dismissal an insult and a sign that they were not needed, that is, that they were weak and worthless, and they departed in great anger, planning to take revenge on Amaziah and to punish him for this insult. Perhaps they were also angry because, by not entering the war, they were deprived of the spoils which they had hoped to obtain from the enemies, and this shows the extent of their pride, since they did not think of the possibility of their being defeated before the enemies and of some of them dying.

25.5.1.en: Be obedient to God's commandments, even if you are alone in carrying out the commandments; and do not be troubled by the threats of the wicked, for all this is worthless, because God supports you, and no man can prevail against you.

25.6.0.en: The Valley of Salt: A valley south of the Dead Sea and beside it.

25.6.1.en: The children of Seir: The Edomites, the descendants of Esau, who dwell in the mountains of Seir.

25.6.2.en: After Amaziah obeyed God, he advanced with courage and faith, and was able to defeat the armies of the Edomites, and even killed 10,000 warriors of them at the place of the battle, which is the Valley of Salt.

25.7.0.en: The rock (Sela): A fortified stronghold in the mountains of Seir, which the Edomites inhabit, and it lies near the foot of one of their mountains, which is called Mount Hor.

25.7.1.en: Amaziah was dazzled by the fortifications of the Edomites and their mountains, and also their temples, in which they offered human sacrifices; so when he triumphed over them, he imitated their savagery and threw 10,000 of the Edomites, whom he had taken captive, from the top of a fortified stronghold of theirs called the rock (Sela), and they fell dead from the mountain; and this method was known among the savage Edomites.

25.8.0.en: Beth-horon: Two cities, one of them built on a plateau and called Upper Beth-horon, and the other in the valley and called Lower Beth-horon, and they lie on the border between the two kingdoms of Israel and Judah, that is, between the tribes of Ephraim and Benjamin.

25.8.1.en: Samaria: The capital of the kingdom of Israel, and it lies north of Jerusalem at a distance of 40 miles, and east of the Mediterranean at a distance of 25 miles.

25.8.2.en: As a result of the anger of the army of Ephraim, whom Amaziah had dismissed, they attacked the kingdom of Judah on its northern borders, taking advantage of the army of Judah's having gone to fight the Edomites, who dwell south of Judah; and they killed three thousand from the kingdom of Judah and plundered much spoil.

25.8.3.en: God permitted this attack on the kingdom of Judah because Amaziah's heart was not perfectly upright; for although he obeyed God, he admired the wicked Edomites and their idols, as will appear from the following verses.

25.9.0.en: Amaziah's evil appeared in his apostasy from God, and he did not stop at admiring the idolaters, but regarded their idols as a great spoil, so he took these images and carried them to Jerusalem and set them up there and bowed down and offered worship to them.

25.9.1.en: This great apostasy shows that Amaziah was superficial in his relationship with God, so at his first test he fell, for he loved the worship of idols. Perhaps the motive for this was his pride, because he had triumphed over the Edomites, and pride darkens the mind. So he took the idols which were not able to protect those who worshipped them, in order to rely on these strange gods and bow down to them instead of God.

25.9.2.en: This shows the extent of the influence of pagan gods on man, for although Amaziah was able to obey God and give up the love of money in the form of the hundred talents of silver, he did not stand before the allurement of the pagan images, but carried them with admiration to Jerusalem and submitted to them.

25.10.0.en: God was angry because of Amaziah's apostasy and sent him a prophet who rebuked him, because he submitted to and worshipped the feeble idols which were not able to protect the Edomites who worshipped them. How could he be dazzled by them? And instead of giving thanks to God in His temple because He had given him victory over the enemies, he bowed down to the feeble pagan gods, that is, to the demons who work in them.

25.11.0.en: Amaziah refused to listen to the voice of God from the mouth of the prophet and interrupted him, saying to him, "Be silent," and even threatened him with death, as he had formerly killed Zechariah the son of Jehoiada, whom God had sent to Joash his father. Here this prophet completed his message to Amaziah and said to him that, because of his refusal to hear the voice of God, he had condemned himself to certain death and destruction on account of his sin.

25.11.1.en: What happened with Amaziah shows that he was in a crisis and in fear of Edom; therefore he obeyed the first prophet, but when he triumphed he became proud and felt that he had no need of God, so he rejected the voice of the second prophet.

26.0.0.en: Gath: One of the five great cities of the Philistines, which are Gath, Ekron, Ashkelon, Ashdod and Gaza, and it lies on the coast of the Mediterranean, north of Ashdod, at a distance of 12 miles.

26.0.1.en: Jabneh: A large city in Palestine, lying south of Joppa, at a distance of 20 km.

26.0.2.en: Ashdod: One of the five great cities of the Philistines, lying north of Gaza, at a distance of 30 km, and it is midway between Gaza and Joppa.

26.0.3.en: The Philistines submitted to King Jehoshaphat and brought him gifts (ch. 17:11), but they took advantage of the weakness of Jehoram his son, because of his departure from God, and attacked him, and took his wives, his children and his possessions (ch. 21:16). But when Uzziah relied on God, he fought the Philistines, who dwell south of the kingdom of Judah toward the coast of the Mediterranean, and attacked three of their great cities, which are Gath, Jabneh and Ashdod, and broke down their walls and took them, and was even able also to build cities belonging to him in those regions. This was his first success.

26.1.0.en: Gur-baal: A region inhabited by Arabs, lying south of Beersheba, that is, south of the kingdom of Judah, and it used to worship Baal, so it was called by this name.

26.1.1.en: The Mehunims: A tribe of the Edomites dwelling in the mountains of Seir, which lie south of the kingdom of Judah. The second success which Uzziah achieved was his victory over other places of the Philistines and the Arabs dwelling in Gur-baal and the Mehunims dwelling in the mountains of Seir. And when the Ammonites submitted to him, they gave him gifts to appease him. The influence and authority of Uzziah extended to the borders of Egypt, that is, he gained greatness and power, so all the nations feared him, until he reached the borders of the mighty kingdom of Egypt.

26.2.0.en: The corner gate: It lies in the northwest of the city of Jerusalem.

26.2.1.en: The valley gate: It lies in the southwest of the city of Jerusalem.

26.2.2.en: Uzziah's third success was his fortifying of Jerusalem, for he built towers in the wall of Jerusalem, at the corner gate and the valley gate, that is, he rebuilt the wall of Jerusalem, which Joash king of Israel had broken down in his war with Amaziah, the father of Uzziah (2 Chr 26:9).

26.3.0.en: Carmel: Its meaning is the fruitful garden, and it is a fertile land lying south of the kingdom of Judah.

26.3.1.en: Uzziah's fourth success was his building of towers in the wilderness of Judah, and his digging of wells to help in the grazing and care of the sheep, because he owned much cattle in the valleys of Judah and as far as the coast of the Mediterranean. And Uzziah's fifth success was his attention to agriculture, for he loved it, so he cared for the various crops in the fertile lands of his kingdom, such as Carmel and in many places of the kingdom, and he had many farmers who tended these crops.

26.4.1.en: The ruler: An officer of high rank.

26.4.2.en: Uzziah's sixth success was his forming a large army whose number was three hundred and seven thousand five hundred soldiers (307,500 soldiers), and they were divided into divisions, so they moved in order, under the command of the king's scribe and two of his military commanders. It is understood from this that Uzziah established a new system and divided his army into divisions, so that they would go out to war company by company according to this system, while the other companies remained to protect the state in careful order. Uzziah was a military thinker, distinguished from the kings who preceded him.

26.4.3.en: And he had two thousand six hundred commanders who led his great army.

26.5.0.en: Shields: The plural of shield, a defensive weapon consisting of a piece of wood.

26.5.1.en: Helmets: The plural of helmet, a metal covering placed on the head of the fighting soldier to protect it.

26.5.2.en: Habergeons: The plural of habergeon, a metal garment which the warrior wears on his chest down to his knees.

26.5.3.en: Bows: The plural of bow, by which arrows are shot.

26.5.4.en: Slings: The plural of sling, a leather instrument in which small stones are placed to be hurled far away and strike the enemies, as David did with Goliath.

26.5.5.en: Engines: The plural of engine (catapult), an ancient war machine with which stones and balls of fire are thrown to break down the walls of cities and burn them.

26.5.6.en: Uzziah was concerned to arm his army with various weapons, whether for the individual warrior, to defend him, such as shields and habergeons, or for attacking the enemies, such as spears and bows and slings. Likewise the great war machines, such as catapults, which had been invented at a time before Uzziah, but he took care to develop them by means of inventors from his army, that is, he had an army armed with the latest weapons.

26.5.7.en: Uzziah was distinguished by many talents, and he succeeded in all fields, as we mentioned in the previous verses, so that his knowledge, skill and strength spread and people spoke of them among the nations around him, like Solomon his forefather, because the power of God that helped him appeared wonderful and mighty in the eyes of all, and he became strong and successful in all that he did. But unfortunately he fell into pride after this, and made himself a priest, and dared to enter the sanctuary, where none enters but the priests, so the Lord struck him with leprosy and he was separated from the people because of his uncleanness, as will appear in the following verses of this chapter.

26.5.8.en: When the grace of God given to you increases, may your heart be lifted up with abundant thanksgiving, lest Satan deceive you and you think that you are something and become proud toward people and God, and so lose everything.

26.6.s.en: (3) The sin, leprosy and death of Uzziah

26.6.0.en: When God blessed King Uzziah and he became strong and prospered in the various fields of administering the kingdom, he became proud and did not ascribe the glory to God, but felt that he was an outstanding king and could do everything, so that he dared to consider that he had the right to enter the sanctuary, like the rest of the priests, and he entered to burn incense on the altar of incense, before the Holy of Holies.

26.7.0.en: The high priest, who was Azariah, was taken by surprise at Uzziah's bursting into the sanctuary, and he was very angry, and so were all the priests with him who were serving in the temple, so Azariah entered after Uzziah with eighty priests, to bring him out of the sanctuary. They commanded him to go out of the sanctuary and informed him that it was not his right to enter, since he was not a priest (Ex 30:7, Deut 33:10). But unfortunately he did not listen to the warnings of the priests not to enter, and perhaps he felt that the prohibition of entering applied to the people but did not apply to him, since the king, in his view, is greater than the priests.

26.7.1.en: It is clear that Uzziah forgot what happened to Korah and his company, who dared to assume the priesthood in the days of Moses and Aaron, so the earth split open and swallowed them (Num 16:35). It is understood from this that Uzziah wanted to combine the dignity of the king and the dignity of the priesthood in his person, and this was not his right, and no one can combine these two dignities except Christ Himself, who is King of kings and the High Priest of the New Covenant, who offered the sacrifice of Himself on the Cross.

26.8.0.en: Wroth: Became violently angry or enraged.

26.8.1.en: King Uzziah was enraged because of the priests' command to him to go out of the sanctuary, for, because of his pride, he was not accustomed to anyone's commanding him; everyone must submit to him, but he submits to no one. Uzziah had taken hold of a censer to burn incense on the altar of incense, like the priests, and since he did not submit to God and resisted in rebellion, God struck him with leprosy immediately, and a white spot appeared on his forehead, so the priests drove him out of the sanctuary, and he himself was very afraid, for he knew that he had been struck with leprosy and had become unclean from the Lord, and that he must be set apart, not only from the temple, but from all the people.

26.8.2.en: The historian Josephus says that the earthquake which occurred in the days of Uzziah and is mentioned in (Amos 1:1) and (Zech 14:5) took place at this time, when Uzziah was struck with leprosy. Josephus also says that the roof of the temple split open and a ray of the sun entered and fell on the face of Uzziah, so his leprosy appeared plainly before all the priests, which made them drive him quickly out of the temple, and Uzziah was in great terror.

26.8.3.en: Uzziah tried in pride to seize the dignity of the priesthood alongside the dignity of the kingship, but he lost both, just as Adam and Eve tried to obtain new knowledge apart from God by eating of the forbidden tree, and so lost their place in Paradise and their knowledge of God.

26.8.4.en: We see Uzziah becoming proud and rebelling against the priests in his entering the sanctuary, but God struck him with leprosy, so he came under the authority of the priests, who examined him and found him a leper, and drove him out and set him apart.

26.8.5.en: Pride makes man lose his true dignity, so that he becomes despised and rejected by God, and the angels and saints grieve over him. Therefore your humility and your thanksgiving to God protect you from the fall of the proud devil, and you will be able to taste the love of God.

26.9.0.en: The priests set Uzziah apart in a house by himself, which they called the house of sickness, in which those afflicted with the disease of leprosy are confined, and he remained afflicted with this disease until the end of his life. Perhaps this was a proof of his uncleanness and of God's rejection of him, and consequently he could not mingle with the people, so his son Jotham reigned in his place, and thus Uzziah, who had been proud, was humbled, so that all the people might know the seriousness of pride.

26.10.0.en: The rest of the acts and life of Uzziah were written by Isaiah the prophet, who was his contemporary. Then Uzziah died, and they did not honor him like the rest of the kings, but buried him in the field of the burial ground of the kings, because he was unclean with his leprosy; then Jotham reigned alone after the death of his father, because he had been reigning for a long time with his father during his sickness.
